A notion is a thought, idea, or concept — something that lives in the mind. So, something notional belongs to the world of ideas and concepts rather than to concrete, practical reality. It exists "in theory" or "on paper," but the real world may tell a different story.

The key tension the word carries is this: there is often a gap between the notional version of something and the actual version. The notional version is tidy and theoretical; the real version may be messier, different in practice, or may not fully exist at all.
Meaning 1: Existing Only in Theory, Not in Reality

This is the most common use. Something notional has been designated, assigned, or agreed upon as a concept — but it doesn't fully hold up in the real world.

Examples:

  • "The treaty gave the rebel group notional control over the northern province." — On paper, they had control. In practice, the region was contested and ungoverned.
  • "He had a notional budget of $5,000 for the project, though everyone knew the actual costs would be far higher." — The figure existed as a planning number, not as a reflection of reality.
  • "The country achieved notional independence in 1960, but foreign powers still directed its economy." — Independence existed as a concept and a label; real self-governance did not.

You will very often see "notional" paired with words like value, control, authority, independence, figure, price — all things that can exist as official designations while the reality is quite different.
Meaning 2: Vague, Speculative, or at the Idea Stage

Notional can describe plans, timelines, or proposals that are approximate, unconfirmed, or still just floating ideas — not yet grounded in firm decisions or facts.

Examples:

  • "We have a notional plan for the event, but nothing has been confirmed yet."
  • "The architect sketched a notional layout for the new building — just to give the client a rough sense of the space."
  • "Her retirement date was notional; she hadn't actually decided."

Here, "notional" signals: don't take this as fixed or final. It's a placeholder, a starting point, a rough shape of an idea.
Meaning 3: In Finance — Notional Value or Notional Amount

This is a very precise, technical use you'll encounter frequently in finance, economics, and business writing.

In financial contracts — especially instruments like derivatives, swaps, and options — the notional value (also called the notional amount or notional principal) is the theoretical face value used to calculate payments. Crucially, this is not the actual amount of money that changes hands.

Here's a simple example: Suppose two banks enter into an interest rate swap with a notional principal of $10 million. Neither bank actually pays the other $10 million. Instead, they exchange interest payments calculated based on that $10 million. The $10 million is a reference number — it exists only as the agreed-upon base for the math, not as real cash being transferred.

This is why the word "notional" fits perfectly: the value is real as a concept and as a calculating tool, but it is not real as money that moves.

  • "The total notional value of the derivatives market runs into the hundreds of trillions of dollars — far exceeding the actual GDP of the world."

When you read about financial markets and see astronomically large figures, they are almost always notional values, not actual money in circulation.

In language study, "notional" refers to meaning or concept, as opposed to grammatical structure or function.

A notional definition defines something by what it means. The classic example is the definition of a noun many of us learned in school: "A noun is a person, place, or thing." That is a notional definition — it tells you what nouns refer to conceptually. A formal definition, by contrast, describes how a noun behaves in a sentence (it can be a subject or object, it takes plural endings, etc.).

Notional grammar is an approach to describing language that organizes words and categories around their meanings — what they express conceptually — rather than around their structural roles. It's the older, more intuitive approach to grammar, and it's been debated by linguists who prefer more rigorous structural analysis.
Meaning 5: Fanciful or Whimsical (Older / Literary Use)

In older English texts and literature, calling someone's ideas — or the person themselves — "notional" carried the flavour of overly imaginative, full of whims, or impractically theoretical. It suggested someone who lived too much in the world of notions and not enough in the world of facts and practical realities.

This meaning is rarely used in modern writing, but you may come across it in 18th- or 19th-century literature. If you do, think of it as: "fanciful, airy, not grounded in reality."

Every use of "notional" shares the same thread: it points away from the concrete and actual, toward the conceptual and theoretical. Whether it's a notional figure in a budget (theoretical), a notional plan (vague and unconfirmed), a notional financial value (a reference number, not real cash), a notional grammar definition (based on concept, not structure), or a notional idea in old literature (fanciful and impractical) — the word consistently marks something as belonging to the world of ideas, not the world of things.

Whenever you encounter "notional," ask yourself: "What would the real or actual version of this look like?" That question will almost always reveal the gap the word is pointing to — the gap between the concept and the reality. The notional version is the conceptual, theoretical, on-paper one; the actual version is what truly exists or happens.

The most natural antonyms of notional are actual, real, concrete, and tangible. Its closest synonyms, depending on context, include theoretical, hypothetical, conceptual, abstract, putative, and nominal (though each of these has its own distinct shade of meaning).
